newsitem.title: USA: U.S., Japan face tough negotiations on insurance.
newsitem.headline: U.S., Japan face tough negotiations on insurance.

text.p: U.S. and Japanese trade negotiators are set to hold a round of talks Friday and Saturday on a long-simmering dispute over insurance deregulation in Japan.

A U.S. trade official told reporters on Thursday that he was hopeful the two sides could settle their differences by a December 15 deadline. But he said negotiators, who are still far apart on key issues after several rounds of talks, faced some long and difficult negotiations.

"We've got a lot of work to do, it is going to be difficult," said the trade official, who spoke to reporters on the condition he not be identified. He said the Japanese have "dug in" on their position concerning primary life and casualty insurance deregulation, which is a main concern for the United States.
Senior U.S. trade negotiator Ira Shapiro and Japan's Eisuke Sakakibara, director-general of the Finance Ministry's International Finance Bureau, will lead the negotiations in San Francisco.
The U.S. official expressed doubt that the dispute would be resolved during the two days of talks, but expressed hope that progress could be made.
"Both sides have a strong desire to solve this problem," he said.

"The ball is substantially in Japan's court," the official said. Tokyo removed a number of issues in September, and the U.S. official said they have to be put back into play if there is to be any progress during the two days of talks.

The United States wants Japan to live up to a 1994 agreement that calls for deregulation of the primary sector dominated by big Japanese firms before deregulation of the so-called third sector, speciality insurance, which is dominated by foreign companies.
Tokyo earlier this year had signalled that it wanted to move on third sector deregulation first, but put on hold those plans to continue talks with the United States.

The U.S. official said a major sticking point is automobile insurance and U.S. desires for more flexibility in pricing. That would allow foreign firms to compete more effectively in the Japanese market and give some Japanese consumers a break on premiums, U.S. officials said.
Despite difficulties faced by negotiators, the official said he was somewhat optimistic the dispute could be settled.
He would not say whether the United States would pursue a complaint in the World Trade Organisation or move to impose unilateral sanctions if talks failed to produce an agreement.
"We have all options open if the agreement fails," the official said.
